title: Is Adobe Flash Still Around? Flash Player in 2026
body:
Adobe Flash Player reached end of life on December 31, 2020, and Adobe began blocking Flash content on January 12, 2021. Adobe still owns Flash but no longer ships it: an enterprise build now comes from Wipro, which took over the work from Harman, and a mainland China build from Zhongcheng Network Technology reached version 34.0.0.380 in June 2026. The authoring tool survives as Adobe Animate, which Adobe put into maintenance mode in February 2026 after saying it would retire the app.

Quick facts
Launched
1996 as FutureSplash Animator, renamed Macromedia Flash 1.0
Owner today
Adobe, which bought Macromedia for about $3.4 billion in 2005
Status today
Discontinued. Flash Player ended December 31, 2020 and was blocked from January 12, 2021
Still shipping
Wipro for enterprise licensees, and a China build at 34.0.0.380 in June 2026
Content preserved
More than 200,000 web games and applications at Flashpoint Archive

Where did Flash come from before Macromedia bought it?

Flash did not start at Macromedia, and it did not start on the web. It began at FutureWave Software, a small San Diego company founded in 1993 by Jonathan Gay and Charlie Jackson. Their first product was SmartSketch, a vector drawing program written for pen computers running the PenPoint operating system.

Pen computing collapsed before SmartSketch found an audience. GO Corporation's PenPoint tablets went nowhere, the EO Personal Communicator line was discontinued, and FutureWave was left with a good drawing program and no market to sell it into.

Gay rebuilt the program around the thing that was growing instead. He added frame-by-frame animation and a browser plug-in for playback, and shipped it in 1996 as FutureSplash Animator. Two customers made it matter: Microsoft used it for MSN, and Disney Online used it for its subscription children's service. Macromedia bought FutureWave soon after and renamed the product Macromedia Flash 1.0, a name taken from the end of Future and the start of Splash.

Accounts differ on the exact month. Gay's own history puts the first shipment in mid-1996 and the breakthrough in August of that year, while contemporary write-ups date the Macromedia deal to either December 1996 or January 1997.

How did Flash take over web video?

The decision that mattered was the distribution model, not the software. The Flash Player plug-in was free for anyone to download. The authoring tool was not. Give away the player, sell the tool, and within a few years the plug-in sat on almost every desktop that had a browser.

The tool got more capable every year. Flash 4 in 1999 added a scripting language and MP3 streaming. Flash 5 in 2000 introduced ActionScript. Flash MX in 2002 added video, which turned out to be the most consequential feature Macromedia ever shipped.

Before Flash video, watching anything online meant QuickTime, RealPlayer or Windows Media Player, each with its own codecs and its own failures. Flash video replaced all three with one player that was already installed. When YouTube launched in February 2005 it was built on Flash video, and Vimeo, Dailymotion and Hulu followed. Neopets, Club Penguin and thousands of browser games ran on the same plug-in.

The side effect was a design convention. All-Flash corporate sites opened on a loading bar and a Skip Intro button, because the whole page was one compiled file rather than a document a browser could read.

Why did Adobe pay $3.4 billion for Macromedia?

On April 18, 2005, Adobe announced a definitive agreement to buy Macromedia in an all-stock transaction valued at about $3.4 billion. Macromedia stockholders were to receive 0.69 shares of Adobe common stock for each Macromedia share, which worked out to $41.86 per share against the closing prices of April 15, 2005, a 25 percent premium. Adobe said it completed the purchase on December 3, 2005.

The logic was tidy. Adobe owned print and design through Photoshop, Illustrator and InDesign. Macromedia owned the web through Flash, Dreamweaver and Fireworks. Together they would hold the whole pipeline.

Adobe rebranded the product Adobe Flash and pushed it past the browser. Adobe AIR let Flash applications run as desktop software. Flex targeted enterprise business applications. The plan was for Flash to be the runtime for everything: websites, video, games, phones and desktops.

It nearly worked. Newgrounds became the center of Flash animation and browser gaming, and Homestar Runner ran entirely on the plug-in. For most of the 2000s, choosing Flash was not a bet on a vendor. It was the default.

Why did Steve Jobs refuse to put Flash on the iPhone?

The iPhone shipped in 2007 without Flash, and Apple never added it. On April 29, 2010, Steve Jobs published an open letter titled "Thoughts on Flash" that explained why, and it did more damage to Adobe than any competitor managed.

Jobs listed six objections: Flash was proprietary rather than open, the full-web argument was misleading because video was moving to H.264, Flash was a leading cause of Mac crashes, it drained batteries, it was designed for mouse rollovers rather than touch, and open standards could do the same work. "Flash was created during the PC era," he wrote, and argued that standards built for the mobile era would win on phones and on PCs too.

Critics noted that Apple had a commercial motive as well, since Flash would have been an application platform outside the App Store. Both things were true. Adobe spent 18 months trying to prove the technical case wrong, then stopped: in November 2011 it ended development of Flash Player for mobile browsers.

Security finished the argument. In July 2015, after Flash zero-days surfaced in the leaked Hacking Team archive, Facebook chief security officer Alex Stamos wrote: "It is time for Adobe to announce the end-of-life date for Flash." Two years later, Adobe set one.

Who owns Adobe Flash today, and where does it still run?

Adobe still owns Flash. It just does not ship it. Adobe announced the end on July 25, 2017, in a statement issued with Apple, Facebook, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla: "we will stop updating and distributing the Flash Player at the end of 2020 and encourage content creators to migrate any existing Flash content to these new open formats." Flash Player reached end of life on December 31, 2020, and from January 12, 2021 Adobe blocked Flash content from running in the player at all.

Two licensed exceptions survive. Enterprise customers outside mainland China can license a supported build, numbered in the 50.x range, from Wipro, whose connected services team took the work over from Harman in 2025. Zhongcheng Network Technology distributes the mainland China build, which kept its own version line and reached 34.0.0.380 on June 9, 2026. That build refuses to start outside China.

The authoring tool outlived the plug-in. Flash Professional was renamed Adobe Animate in 2016 and is still sold. Adobe almost ended that too: in early February 2026 it told customers Animate was being retired, animators and studios pushed back hard, and within days Adobe reversed course. "We are not discontinuing or removing access to Adobe Animate," the company said in a statement reported by TechCrunch on February 4, 2026. Animate now sits in maintenance mode, which Adobe defines as continued security and bug fixes with no new features.

Can you still play old Flash games and animations?

Yes, and more of them than at any point since 2020. The original plug-in is not the route. Ruffle, an open-source Flash Player emulator written in Rust that runs in the browser through WebAssembly, reimplements playback without any Adobe code. Newgrounds began sponsoring Ruffle in 2019 and swapped its own Flash embeds for it, so much of the site's pre-2007 library loads with no plug-in at all.

Flashpoint Archive is the bigger effort. The volunteer project has been collecting since December 2017 and now holds more than 200,000 web games and applications covering Flash, Shockwave, Silverlight, Java applets, the Unity Web Player and over a hundred other browser technologies. It ships as a downloadable launcher that plays the files offline, and the Internet Archive runs its own Flash library with Ruffle embedded in the page.

Preservation is not complete. Titles that called a server for scores, advertising or multiplayer often cannot be fully restored, and some were never captured before the sites hosting them shut down. ActionScript 3 content, which covers most of the later and more ambitious work, is still the weakest area for Ruffle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Adobe Flash Player still available to download in 2026?

Not from Adobe. Adobe stopped distributing Flash Player when it reached end of life on December 31, 2020, and removed the download links. Two licensed builds still exist in 2026: an enterprise version from Wipro for companies outside mainland China, and a China build from Zhongcheng Network Technology, at version 34.0.0.380 as of June 2026, that will not run elsewhere.

Why did Adobe kill Flash?

Adobe ended Adobe Flash because open standards caught up and the plug-in became a security liability. HTML5 video, CSS animation, WebGL and JavaScript covered what Flash did without a plug-in, while Flash was one of the most exploited programs on the internet. Apple never allowed it on the iPhone after 2007, Adobe stopped building it for mobile browsers in November 2011, and on July 25, 2017 Adobe set the end-of-life date of December 31, 2020 alongside Apple, Facebook, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla.

How do you play Flash games in 2026?

Two routes work. Ruffle, a free open-source emulator, plays many Flash files directly in a modern browser and is built into sites such as Newgrounds. Flashpoint Archive, which has been preserving browser content since December 2017, offers a desktop launcher with more than 200,000 games and applications that run offline, including Shockwave and Java titles that were never Flash at all.
